turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, Mr. Hale. I'm Dr. Alvarez. Nobody's rushing you, so what brings you in?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing. I'm fine. Karen, my wife, made this appointment, and I figured I'd show up so she'd quit nagging.
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): You came, and that matters. What does she keep nagging you about?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): She says I don't do anything anymore. I think she just wants a project. I'm fine.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Maybe. Or she's seeing something you're waving off. How have the days actually been?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Days are days. Hey, did you catch that rain on the way over? The lot out front is basically a pond.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): I did. I almost lost a shoe in that puddle by the entrance.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, somebody should fix the drain. My grandson Eli had a little league game Saturday and they called it in the third inning. Mud everywhere.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's a shame. How old is Eli?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Eight. He plays second base, or he tries. Mostly he picks dandelions, and Karen films the whole thing like it's the World Series.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Eight is a fun age. Did they get the game in another day?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday, and then it poured again. We sat in the car with gas station donuts. He was thrilled. I was just the guy with the keys.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Gas station donuts in a dry car. That's a win when you're eight.

[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Glazed, and my truck seat is a crime scene. Biscuit, our beagle, sheds all over it too. Eli named him. I already told Karen I'm not sitting through another rain delay, coach's emails or not.
[SEG0015] person_1 (DOCTOR): I don't blame you. Sounds like a whole weekend of wet bleachers.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): Pretty much. And 35 was stopped dead by that river bridge construction. Took forty minutes to go two miles, some guy in a red pickup honking the whole way.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): That project has been a mess for months. I leave early just to dodge it.
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): You and everybody else. I almost rolled the window down and said something. Didn't, though.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Probably for the best. I do want to come back to you, though, not the traffic. When she says you don't do anything, what does a regular day look like now?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I get up. I drink coffee. I watch whatever's on. It's not a crisis.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Coffee and the TV. Are you sleeping at night, or is that part of what's going on?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): The layoff was the real kick in the teeth. Meridian Logistics, night-shift supervisor for twelve years, and they outsourced the whole crew the week before Thanksgiving.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Twelve years is a long time. I'm sorry they did that. I was asking about your sleep, though. How are the nights?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Nights are whatever. I just lie there. It's not like I need a sleeping pill. I'm fine.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): Lying there awake isn't really fine, even if that's the line you've been using. How long has that been going on?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The lying awake? I don't know. A while. I couldn't tell you the day it started.
[SEG0027] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's alright. Would you call it weeks, or more like months?
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Months. The bad sleep's been since the layoff, I guess, that week before Thanksgiving. So, what, four months, five. Somewhere in there.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): So around four or five months. When you do fall asleep, do you stay asleep?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): Karen keeps the thermostat on sixty-eight. I told her that's ridiculous, I'm not paying to freeze. Now she wants a space heater.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sixty-eight is chilly if the bill's in your name. About the sleep, though. Do you wake up before you mean to?
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. Like three or four in the morning, and then I'm just staring at the ceiling. Maybe four hours total. Five if I'm lucky.
[SEG0033] person_1 (DOCTOR): Four or five hours and up that early will wear you down. How's your energy during the day?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): It's fine. I mean, I'm a little dragged out, but who isn't. Nothing dramatic.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): A little dragged out. Is that most days?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Most days, yeah. I used to mess around after shift. Now the couch wins. That's me being lazy, not some disease.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulling back isn't the same as lazy. Are there things you used to enjoy that don't interest you now?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): The truck needs brakes and they quoted me eight hundred dollars. I'm not made of money since the layoff.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Eight hundred is steep with no paycheck. We'll leave the truck. Fishing, ballgames, friends. Does any of that still feel worth it?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Not really. I used to fish on Sundays with my brother. I haven't been since, I don't know, Christmas, and I don't even want to. I just tell him I'm busy.
[SEG0041] person_1 (DOCTOR): Since around Christmas, and the want is gone. Along with that, have you felt down or hopeless, or is it mainly that you don't care?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I wouldn't say hopeless. I'm not sitting around crying or anything. I just don't care about much. Karen calls it depressed, I call it a slump.

[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Okay. A long slump, with the sleep and the energy and the not caring. I need to ask something straight, and a no is a perfectly good answer. Have you had any thoughts of hurting yourself, or that you'd rather not be alive?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Absolutely not. I'm not going to hurt myself, that thought has not crossed my mind. I'm just tired of all of it.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): I appreciate how clear that was. Has your appetite changed, or your weight?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I eat. Same as always. Maybe more junk at night, but that's nothing. Weight's the same as far as I know.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright, eating and weight about steady. Any worry, heart racing, feeling on edge?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I'm not anxious. If anything I'm the opposite, just flat. Karen says I don't even argue anymore.
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): Flat, not on edge. Do you drink in the evenings, or take anything to try to sleep?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): A beer with the ballgame, sometimes two. Not every night, and not to knock myself out. I don't smoke either. Never have.
[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): So a beer or two with the game, not nightly, and no smoking. Do you take any medicine at all, even over the counter?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Karen's on a thyroid pill, but that's hers, not mine. I tried her melatonin once and it didn't do a thing, so I didn't take it again.
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): Got it, nothing of yours on a regular basis. Any big health problems, or surgeries?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Healthy as a horse. Had my appendix out when I was nineteen, that's it. Blood pressure's always come back normal on those drugstore machines.

[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): Appendix at nineteen, otherwise healthy by your account. When I put the months of poor sleep, the low energy, and losing interest after the layoff side by side, it looks like a depressive episode. I'm not locking that in as a final label today.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): I hate that word. But... yeah. It's been worse than I tell Karen. I just didn't want to make it a thing.

[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Saying it here counts. Sertraline is a medicine I use for this sometimes, but I am not starting any medication today. I'd rather you talk with someone before we even consider a pill.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. I don't want a pill. Talking, I guess I could try. Maybe.

[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll put in a referral to behavioral health, and I want to see you back in this office in four weeks. If your sleep or your mood drops before then, call us instead of waiting. If thoughts of hurting yourself ever show up, go to the ER or call 911.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Alright. Four weeks. I'll tell Karen you didn't say I was crazy.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): You're not crazy. You're exhausted, and it matters. I'll see you in four weeks.
